## About Me

<!-- bio:start -->
I work at the intersection of research transparency, public policy and economics. My main research measures which results in economics go unreported. To do this, I encode pre-registered hypotheses and their findings in a standardized format and track whether each result becomes publicly available. I also work on increasing transparency throughout the evidence-to-policy pipeline, with a focus on policy analysis. Estimates of a policy's costs and impacts should make their assumptions explicit, so that readers can inspect and modify them. I believe economics is entering a new stage in how evidence is reported and used in policy. I aspire to be part of the group of researchers studying and strengthening the link between evidence and policy.

Most recently, I worked at UC Berkeley as a staff researcher. There I developed a framework for transparency in policy analysis, along with interactive demonstrations that let users modify the assumptions behind a policy estimate. I also co-led a three-year project on the reporting of pre-registered results in economics. We tracked over 5,000 hypotheses from pre-registered RCTs and found that fewer than half had a publicly available result 8 to 9 years later. We then ran an RCT with the original research teams to identify the constraints behind unreported results ([my job market paper](https://fhoces.github.io/research.html#job-market-paper)).

Before that, I did my PhD in Public Policy at RAND, with a dissertation on making policy analysis more transparent and reproducible. Before my PhD, I studied economics (BA and master's at U. de Chile, MA at UPenn) and worked in Chile's public sector, evaluating social programs and conducting economic analysis of social policies.
<!-- bio:end -->
